newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia jobs survey change effect gone - ABS.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia jobs survey change effect gone - ABS.

text.p: The Australian Bureau of Statistics examined jobs data in extreme detail to measure the effect of telephone interviewing and finally determine that the problem was only transitional, statisticians said on Friday.

"We used a combination of different methods, some technical methods as well as intuitive methods and checked them against each other," said one senior analyst. "I was struck by the consistency between the different methods."

The telephone effect has had a severe impact on analysts' economic estimates, which have waxed and waned as the distortion in the data was first unknown, then said to have understated jobs growth and now said to have initially understated it and later overstated it.
But the bureau does not intend to correct the figures for the period of the distortion -- August to February.

The statisticians said while they could quantify the telephone effect on such large numbers as employment levels, they could not divide it into small components, such as under-18s looking for part-time employment in the state of Tasmania.
They therefore encourage analysts to correct the major numbers themselves, preferably using trend analysis.
(Such a corrected series is shown in an accompanying report.)
The bureau phased in telephone interviewing from August, each month dropping one panel of respondents approached face-to-face while interviewing one more by telephone.
In February, the survey reached its final configuration in which the newest panel is introduced face-to-face while the older seven panels are interviewed by telephone.

The bureau initially said the cheaper telephone technique would have no noticeable effect but in mid January, having seen five months of phase-in data, it conceded that the change had significantly affected the figures.

But in its February data release on Thursday the bureau said the problem had gone -- the distortion had initially built up to the point that November jobs data was understated by 36,000 to 48,000 but then faded to insignificance in February.

The most obvious method of checking for the effect was to simply compare the overall results it was getting from the two methods during the phase in. As it happened, the telephone method initially produced lower employment numbers.
But the statisticians said they also undertook much more detailed analysis, trying to extract extra little bits of information from individual telephone groups.

Watching the stream of results from each survey group gave the bureau additional confidence to exclude sample noise. (For example, if a particular month produced a big rise that was followed by a big fall, the bureau could be more confident that the rise was less genuine.)

Having so refined the results of each response group the bureau could then, for example, compare the behaviour of telephone respondents with face-to-face respondents, to remove the pattern of results that might be expected as people got used to being surveyed each month.
Such detailed examinations were then checked against the simple comparison between overall telephone and face-to-face results.
In the end, the statisticians said, the pattern of results suggested some kind of initial effect from the introduction of telephone interviewing that settled down after a few months.

The statisticians were unsure of the practical source of the effect but, speculatively, one possibility was interviewers becoming accustomed to the new technique and perhaps being affected by variation in their workloads.
